slides.1.title: Granite: A Fine Soil of Fresh Minerality
slides.1.html:
Granite (Granito) is the most important soil of the mountains of northern and central Portugal, widespread across Minho・Dão・Trás-os-Montes.

🔬 Physical and Chemical Properties of Granite

  • Mineral composition: quartz + feldspar + mica, an acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5)
  • Excellent drainage: weathered granite forms a coarse sandy soil through which water drains quickly, so vines need deep roots to find water
  • Poor, low-yielding: low fertility naturally limits yields but gives high fruit concentration
  • Low heat retention: pale and reflective, cooler than schist, helping to preserve the grapes' natural acidity

🍾 Influence on the Wine

  • Minerality: the fresh mineral character of flint, chalk and mineral water
  • Retained high acidity: cool, well-drained soil lets grapes ripen slowly, preserving natural acidity
  • Light and elegant: wines from granite are usually lighter in body and finer on the palate
  • Key examples: Monção Alvarinho (mineral granite white), Dão Encruzado (complex granite white), Dão Touriga Nacional (elegant and fine)
slides.2.title: Soils × Regions × Wine Styles at a Glance
slides.2.items.0.label: Granite (Granito)
slides.2.items.0.desc: Minho・Dão: cool and mineral, fresh with high acidity, fine and light. Mineral Alvarinho whites, complex Encruzado whites, elegant Touriga Nacional reds
slides.2.items.1.label: Schist (Xisto)
slides.2.items.1.desc: Douro: dark and heat-retaining, vine roots penetrate deep, smoky mineral character and dark fruit. Port and top Douro reds (Barca Velha・Quinta do Crasto)
slides.2.items.2.label: Clay-limestone
slides.2.items.2.desc: Bairrada・Bucelas: good water retention, a high-acid structural backbone, Baga's high tannin and acidity, Arinto's mineral, fresh whites
slides.2.items.3.label: Granite・Gneiss (Alentejo)
slides.2.items.3.desc: Alentejo (especially Portalegre): between the finesse of granite and the heat of the south, producing balanced, mineral southern reds
slides.3.question: Why does Douro's schist (Xisto) soil let vine roots reach as deep as 20 metres?
slides.3.options.0: Schist contains special plant growth hormones
slides.3.options.1: Schist has vertical fissures, and vine roots can penetrate down along them to find deep groundwater
slides.3.options.2: Schist soil is especially loose, so roots grow easily
slides.3.options.3: The mineral content of schist attracts vine roots
slides.3.explanation: Douro's schist is known for its vertical layered fissures, along which vine roots can penetrate 10–20 metres down in search of deep groundwater. This forced deep rooting lets the vines find enough water during summer drought and also increases mineral uptake, which is the source of Port's complex minerality.
slides.4.question: Of Portugal's three main soils, which has the strongest heat retention and contributes most to grape ripeness?
slides.4.explanation: Schist (Xisto) is a dark grey-black, thinly layered metamorphic rock. Its dark colour absorbs heat strongly, taking in plenty of solar radiation by day and releasing it slowly at night, creating a distinctive "geothermal effect". This strong heat retention lets the grapes ripen fully even in the Douro's hot summers, and is an important factor in Port's high sugar levels and rich fruit.
slides.5.message: Congratulations on completing the Portuguese soils and terroir lesson!
slides.5.keyPoints.0: Granite (Minho/Dão): cool and mineral, fresh with high acidity, fine and light, the soul of Alvarinho and Encruzado
slides.5.keyPoints.1: Schist (Douro): dark and heat-retaining, forces roots deep, smoky mineral character, the basis of Port and top Douro reds
slides.5.keyPoints.2: Limestone (Bairrada/Bucelas): water retention and high acidity, a firm backbone, the structural source of Baga and Arinto
slides.5.keyPoints.3: Soil sets the direction of style, but climate and variety matter just as much: together the three make up "terroir"
